bibliographic.title: Responsible AI in practice 2025 global insights from the AI Company Data Initiative
bibliographic.citation_apa: Thomson Reuters Foundation & UNESCO. (2026). Responsible AI in practice 2025: Global insights from the AI Company Data Initiative. Thomson Reuters Foundation & UNESCO. https://doi.org/10.54678/YJWP8855

methodology.method_family: corporate disclosure document analysis with LLM-assisted content parsing against the AICDI framework
methodology.study_design: cross-sectional analysis of voluntary corporate AI governance disclosures
methodology.sample_description: Companies covered by the AI Company Data Initiative (AICDI), assessed through public corporate materials including annual and ESG reports, governance and responsible AI webpages, cybersecurity and privacy policies, and diversity reporting
methodology.sector: multi-sector corporations (technology, telecommunications, banking, chemicals, cement, and other industries represented in case studies)
methodology.technology_context: Corporate-level responsible AI governance disclosure and regulatory landscape mapping; LLM used as an analysis tool to parse source documents against the AICDI survey framework, not as the primary subject of conversational system governance

eligibility.decision_rationale: The publication provides empirical global insights on corporate responsible AI governance, regulatory frameworks, risk management, human oversight, and generative AI regulation through the AICDI initiative. It explicitly uses a large language model to analyze corporate disclosures. However, the provided text contains no evidence on conversational AI systems, chatbots, agents, RAG, guardrails, observability, tracing, handoff, or contestation in deployed conversational LLM applications. It is therefore better suited as foundational/contextual evidence for AI governance in regulated environments than as central evidence on conversational governance.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Confirm publication type (report vs. journal article), peer-review status, and AICDI sample size/statistics from sections not fully extracted (Key Statistics, AICDI dataset breakdown).

appraisal.notes: Strengths include a clearly described disclosure-based methodology and structured thematic findings. The LLM-assisted parsing approach is transparently described, including instructions to populate fields only with explicit evidence and to flag interpretive content. Weaknesses for this review include unclear sample size in the provided excerpts, likely voluntary-disclosure bias, and no conversational-AI operational governance detail.

cerqual.explanation: Findings are coherent with the stated aim of assessing corporate responsible AI practice through public disclosures, but voluntary reporting and LLM-assisted extraction introduce limitations. Relevance to conversational LLM governance is indirect: strong on corporate governance, regulation, and generative AI policy context; weak on conversational system controls and post-deployment oversight.

open_codes: training data and user data rights
coding.theme: Corporate responsible AI governance practice and disclosure
coding.subtheme: Regulatory context and voluntary corporate reporting on AI governance

synthesis.main_claim: Public corporate commitment to AI governance frameworks remains limited and uneven, with gaps between published AI strategies and demonstrated practice, especially around worker protections, ethical issues, and data governance.
synthesis.contribution: Provides a 2025 global empirical snapshot of corporate responsible AI disclosures, maps major AI regulatory developments, and documents how an LLM was used to operationalize structured assessment of public corporate materials against the AICDI framework.
synthesis.limitations: Based on voluntary public disclosures rather than independent verification of deployed AI systems; sample size and full limitation discussion are not available in the provided excerpts; no focus on conversational AI operational controls.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as foundational/contextual evidence for the regulatory and corporate governance backdrop of responsible generative AI in regulated environments. Do not treat as central evidence on conversational LLM governance, guardrails, observability, audit logs, tracing, handoff, or contestation mechanisms.
